items.title: A comparative review of implemented explainable AI techniques in multi-agent systems
items.abstract: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has largely been developed for single-model settings, where the target of explanation is one prediction, model, or decision process. This assumption is limited in multi-agent systems (MAS), where outcomes can depend on coordination, communication, decentralised information, and interaction over time. This paper presents a structured comparative review restricted to studies of implemented and empirically evaluated XAI methods in MAS. Here, implemented means that a concrete explanation mechanism is applied in a MAS and tested. The search covered cooperative, competitive, mixed-motive, planning, ad-hoc teamwork, and LLM-based MAS. The included evidence contains work in cooperative and decentralised MARL, as well as planning-oriented and LLM-based MAS work. The review compares studies by explanatory target (the aspect of the system being explained) and stakeholder orientation (who the explanations are for). Current methods can identify influential agents, summarise policies, interpret local decisions, and diagnose failures, however they struggle to explain how interaction and communication produce a system-level outcome. Future work should therefore develop more interaction-aware, empirically grounded, and human-usable explanations for MAS.

items.title: A Comparative Survey-Based Study of AI Adoption, Code Verification Practices, and Future Career Readiness Among Computing Students and Software Developers in India
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming a useful part of software development, particularly in activities such as writing programs, debugging errors, testing code, and learning programming concepts. This research focuses on how computing students and software professionals in India use AI tools, check AI-generated code, and prepare themselves for changes in the software industry. For this study, information was gathered through a Google Forms questionnaire completed by 113 participants. The participants included undergraduate and postgraduate computing students, working software developers, and IT professionals. The responses were examined using frequency counts, percentages, and comparisons between the respondent groups. The survey results indicate that 96.5% of participants use AI tools for programming-related tasks. At the same time, 65.5% reported that they frequently or very frequently face incorrect or incomplete code generated by AI tools. The responses also show that 57.5% of participants always check AI-generated code before using it. In addition, 89.4% believe that AI will bring significant or moderate changes to the skills needed in future software development. The study indicates that AI tools are becoming common in programming activities, but their outputs still require careful examination. It also highlights the importance of programming fundamentals, problem-solving, code verification, and continuous learning. Overall, AI can assist software professionals, but human understanding and responsibility remain important for producing reliable software.

items.title: A Determinant Model of Employee Performance in the Coal Mining Industry of West Aceh: An Examination of Individual Factors
items.abstract: This research examines the extent to which job satisfaction moderates the impact of Occupational Health and Safety and employee competency on performance outcomes in West Aceh's coal mining sector. Given the demanding, high-risk nature of mining activities, employee performance is crucial to ensuring both operational effectiveness and workplace safety. Optimal performance not only supports organizational productivity but also helps integrate safety standards and technical competencies, maintaining efficiency and resilience in the mining sector. The research population comprises all employees working in the coal mining industry in West Aceh. The study employs a quantitative design with hypothesis testing. The study used non-probability purposive sampling combined with convenience sampling because the researcher could access the most available respondents during the study period, meaning not all population members had an equal chance of selection. The study was conducted between May and June 2026. Primary data were gathered through a survey administered to employees. The analysis used PLS-SEM in SmartPLS 4 and comprised two phases: evaluating the measurement model for convergent and discriminant validity, and assessing the structural model to determine path coefficients, coefficients of determination, effect sizes, and predictive relevance. The analysis indicates that competency and job satisfaction significantly and positively predict employee performance, whereas OHS does not have a statistically significant impact. Subsequent moderation analysis shows that job satisfaction positively moderates the association between competency and performance, while negatively moderating the relationship between OHS and performance.

items.title: A Framework for Assessing Institutional Readiness for Responsible and Sustainable AI Adoption in Higher Education
items.abstract: As higher education institutions increasingly adopt artificial intelligence (AI) across teaching, learning, research, and institutional operations, considerable variation exists in how AI is implemented, governed, and integrated into institutional practice. Although scholarly interest in AI in higher education continues to grow, the intersection of AI and sustainability remains insufficiently explored. Limited research has examined how universities leverage AI to advance sustainability objectives while ensuring the sustainable and responsible development, deployment, and use of AI, or whether they possess the institutional readiness required to support these complementary aims. This study used a Delphi method to develop and validate an expert-informed AI readiness framework for higher education. The framework consists of five interconnected capabilities: strategic, governance, human, sustainability and adaptive capability. Experts in the Delphi discussion emphasised strong foundations in strategic leadership, effective governance, and appropriate infrastructure, as well as human capability, systematic evaluation, and organisational learning. The framework also incorporates Māori values such as Wairuatanga, Tino Rangatiratanga, and Ōritetanga, extending readiness beyond technical and organisational capacity to include ethical, cultural, relational, and equity considerations. Overall, the findings suggest that readiness depends on technology and on aligning AI with institutional priorities, responsibilities, people, cultural context, and sustainability commitments. The framework is intended to provide a conceptual foundation for institutional readiness rather than a prescriptive assessment tool. Nevertheless, its domains and capabilities may serve as the basis for developing indicators, evaluative rubrics, or maturity scales that enable institutions to assess existing capacities, identify developmental priorities, and support strategic planning. Developing and validating such assessment mechanisms represents an important direction for future research.

items.title: A student-centred and technology-enhanced online learning competency framework
items.abstract: This study aimed to develop and validate a student-centred and technology-enhanced competency framework for online learning settings. The framework defines competencies required to shape and support inclusive e-learning and instructional design, data privacy and governance in learning analytics as well as the ethical and responsible integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in e-learning platforms. It comprises four operational competency matrices (exploration, adoption, experience, and leadership), four dimensions (online learning technology, online learning environment, online learning management, and online learning delivery), and four domains (technical, functional, governance, and pedagogical). Each domain includes eight competencies aligned to specific audience (stakeholders) and intended purpose​. The framework emphasises human-centred AI approaches to learning analytics and collaboration among e-learning stakeholders to strengthen student support and educational design practices. The study adopted a mixed-methods research design, supported by Design Science Research and a Delphi validation method. Data were collected through an institutional survey and a Delphi survey. Qualitative methods were used to identify competencies, while quantitative techniques were employed to determine expert competence levels and overall consensus. Validation results revealed an expert competence coefficient of 0.683 (68.3%)​ and an overall expert consensus of 71.4%, ​ indicating a moderate level of expert competence, and a substantial agreement regarding the framework’s structure, competencies validity, coherence, and practical applicability respectively. The study concludes that enhanced and effective online learning requires institutional coordinated competency development through upskilling and reskilling initiatives using subject matter experts. Competencies shall extend beyond functional or technological proficiency to include core and leadership competencies that foster ethics, ​governance, ​ inclusion, and responsible AI adoption. The proposed framework provides a ​ foundation for capacity building to support inclusive, ethical, and data-driven online learning environments in higher education where all students thrive. items.title: A Taxonomy Of Behaviors On Human-AI Communities Foundation Design
items.abstract: In communities where humans and AI agents share work, the record of a decision may identify who approved a result while saying little about who investigated it, who could see it or how other participants used it. This paper proposes five levels of behavioral description. They distinguish epistemic activity, occurring conduct, manifestation, social attribution and normative qualification. An episode can support several descriptions, each with its own evidential requirements. Manifestation merits a distinct level because the same act can leave different evidence for its operator, its intended recipient and a later reviewer. An audit of five deterministic Koinonia simulations finds 21 requests for release. A count based on admitted acts recovers 12 and omits nine documented attempts. Two hypothetical cases extend the analysis to a negotiation over a shared archive and a shift handoff at a food cooperative. The latter distinguishes assigning a volunteer to call a member from reaching the member in time to collect a parcel. The resulting design links descriptions to episodes, identifies the audience or rule behind an attribution and makes disclosure of epistemic work subject to agreement. The simulations establish the consequences of a counting choice within one archive. The value of the taxonomy for live communities remains an empirical question.

items.abstract: Objective Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into medicine, but surgeons’ real-world adoption and perceptions of its benefits and risks remain insufficiently characterized. We assessed AI use, perceived clinical value and concerns, and differences between trainees and attending surgeons. Methods We conducted a national multicenter cross-sectional online survey of surgeons and trainees across nine hospitals, assessing demographics, AI use, clinical value, educational or professional concerns, and attitudes toward integration. Likert items were summarized as medians and interquartile ranges. AI adoption was the primary between-group comparison; others were exploratory and Benjamini-Hochberg-adjusted. Effect estimates include 95% confidence intervals. Results Of 243 respondents, 124 were attendings and 119 trainees; 76.3% used AI in clinical or professional work. Among users, applications included administrative tasks (76.6%), education or literature review (51.1%), research (41.8%), technical skill improvement (30.4%), and clinical decision support (26.6%). Adoption was higher among trainees (83.9% vs 69.1%; absolute risk difference, 14.8 percentage points; 95% CI, 4.1-25.1). Trust in AI as a supportive clinical tool was 51.7%. Concerns about clinical-knowledge atrophy and suppression of trainee learning were reported by 41.7% and 47.1%, respectively. Confidence in overriding AI recommendations did not differ significantly, but response distributions did: trainees more often selected “Don’t know” (28.8% vs 13.8%; P = 0.002). Conclusions AI is used in surgery, predominantly for administrative, educational, and information-related tasks rather than direct clinical decision-making. Despite higher trainee adoption, clinical trust remained modest. Trainee uncertainty about overriding AI recommendations is hypothesis-generating. Further evaluation should guide AI integration into surgical practice and education while preserving critical appraisal and independent clinical reasoning.

items.title: Advancing university teachers’ digital competence through AI pedagogy and emerging technologies for sustainable higher education in Paraguay
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and emerging digital technologies is reshaping higher education, creating new opportunities to advance Sustainable Development Goal 4 (SDG 4) through innovative, inclusive, and technology-enhanced teaching practices. However, the successful adoption of AI depends largely on university teachers’ digital competence and their ability to integrate these technologies pedagogically, ethically, and responsibly. This study investigates the extent to which AI pedagogy and emerging technologies can strengthen university teachers’ digital competence in Paraguay and contribute to sustainable educational transformation. A sequential explanatory mixed-methods design was employed. In the quantitative phase, data were collected from 800 university teachers across multiple Paraguayan higher education institutions using a questionnaire assessing five dimensions of digital competence and AI-related competencies. The qualitative phase included semi-structured interviews, reflective teaching portfolios, and classroom observations to further explore educators’ experiences with AI-supported teaching. The findings reveal that although participants demonstrate moderate levels of overall digital competence, important deficiencies remain in pedagogical content creation, digital security, AI literacy, ethical decision-making, and the responsible use of generative AI. Conversely, teachers who incorporated AI-supported pedagogical strategies—including adaptive learning environments, learning analytics, AI-assisted assessment, and collaborative digital platforms—reported improvements in instructional design, personalized learning, formative assessment, student engagement, and teaching efficiency. Qualitative analyses further identified four interconnected themes: AI as a pedagogical facilitator, ethical challenges associated with AI integration, the need for continuous professional development, and the role of AI in promoting inclusive and sustainable educational practices. The study contributes empirical evidence from the Paraguayan higher education context and proposes a contextualized framework for integrating AI pedagogy into institutional digital transformation strategies. The findings provide practical implications for university leaders, policymakers, and teacher education programs by supporting evidence-based policies that strengthen educators’ digital competence, promote the ethical governance of AI, and advance sustainable higher education aligned with SDG 4.

items.title: Agentic Virtual Cells (AVCs): From Cell Models to Auditable Discovery Systems
items.abstract: Virtual cells, computational models that predict how cellular state changes under genetic, chemical or environmental perturbation, are increasingly built, queried and revised by artificial intelligence (AI) agents rather than by human modellers alone. Here we argue that the consequential change is not a further increase in the capacity of any single model but the explicit implementation of an operator layer: the decisions about which model to trust, which evidence to add and which experiment to run that human modellers have always made implicitly. We define an agentic virtual cell as a coupled system of a predictive cell model, an agent policy, an evidence ledger and a laboratory interface, and we distinguish four couplings through which agents and virtual cells interact: agents use models as instruments, build models, plan with models as world models and learn from models as verifiers. Drawing on the 2025 Virtual Cell Challenge, recent benchmark disputes and the first agent-built and agent-operated systems, we show that current performance limits arise jointly from model capacity, coverage of biological context and evaluation design, and that agents can relieve the second but cannot, by orchestration alone, create causal identifiability. We propose a two-tier evaluation of model outputs and agent trajectories and state five falsifiable predictions for the next five years.

items.title: AI for Artists - 7 Deadly Sins & 7 Heavenly Virtues - Public Talk at Fine Arts Society Milton by Amanda Tkaczyk
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, Your Art, and You is an introductory AI literacy talk for visual artists, presented by Amanda Tkaczyk to the Fine Arts Society of Milton on November 25, 2026. The slides explain the difference between generative and non-generative AI and explore where artists encounter AI in creative work, research, professional development, arts administration, and community organizing. Using the Seven Deadly Sins and Seven Heavenly Virtues as a discussion framework, the talk considers how AI affects artists’ choices, creative communities, and the institutions that shape AI use. Topics include copyright and ownership, labour and environmental impacts, bias, privacy, disclosure, and trust. The talk also explores how AI might support critical feedback, artistic collaboration, and cultural preservation. items.title: AI for economics and the economics of AI
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is both a toolkit for economic research, in measurement, prediction, identification, and computation, and an economic force acting on production, work, and growth. This survey connects the two roles through intelligence as a produced factor: cognitive services an algorithm makes from data and compute, traded separately from human labor. We review the toolkit and the evidence on labor markets, market power, and governance, then follow the production chain. The data must be recorded and can be reused to train the next model; the algorithm predicts reliably only where the process behind the record is stationary and ergodic. Deployment is wide but uneven across occupations and tasks, and cheap generation outruns verification under goals no instruction fully specifies. These properties compound: errors made where the record is silent can pass unverified, re-enter training, and become harder to anticipate when the factor acts as an agent. The Middle-Intelligence Trap is the hypothesis that this feedback persists while expertise and corrective investment lag. Descriptive evidence from 253 U.S. occupations links AI usage concentrated on core tasks to lower employment growth; the association is conditional and absent from payroll data. A stylized model identifies a verification externality when corrections reach later training.

items.title: AI-Driven Digital Twins and Cyber-Physical Systems 2.0 for Human–Robot Collaboration in Industry 5.0 and Beyond: A Narrative Review
items.abstract: This article provides a comprehensive overview of digital twins (DTs) and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled Cyber-Physical Systems 2.0 (CPS 2.0), focused on human–robot collaboration within the context of Industry 5.0 and subsequent stages of industrial development. The paper analyzes the convergence of AI, collaborative robotics, real-time data analytics, and the integration of the virtual and physical realms, which enables the creation of intelligent, adaptive, and human-centric industrial environments. It discusses fundamental architectures, supporting technologies, and emerging application areas, such as predictive maintenance, task planning in collaborative systems, ergonomic assessment, intelligent safety monitoring, and adaptive manufacturing. Particular attention is given to the inclusion of the human element, eXplainable AI (XAI), autonomous decision-making, and the continuous synchronization between physical assets and their digital counterparts. The authors critically identify scientific and practical gaps concerning interoperability, cybersecurity, data quality, system reliability, scalability, and human trust. Furthermore, the paper outlines directions for future research, including generative AI (GenAI), trustworthy autonomous systems, and sustainable industrial intelligence. The conclusions presented offer a conceptual foundation for the development of resilient, safe, efficient, and human-centric production ecosystems that extend beyond the framework of Industry 5.0.

items.title: AI-Driven IT Service Management in Large Enterprises: Incident Resolution, Service Delivery, and Operational Resilience
items.abstract: Enterprise IT has grown too large and too interconnected for manual, rule-based IT service management (ITSM) to keep up. Artificial intelligence for IT operations (AIOps) promises faster detection, routing, diagnosis and recovery, but how much of that holds up in real operations? This structured narrative review examines 12 peer-reviewed primary studies of production AIOps, incident-management and service-desk systems published between 2019 and 2026, alongside four earlier reviews and one industry briefing. It asks how far AI improves incident resolution and service delivery, what makes it work, whether it builds resilience, and how it should be governed. The gains are real but narrow. Ticket routing, diagnosis and outage assessment improve, and two deployments report shorter times to root cause or resolution. Much depends on telemetry quality, dependency knowledge, workflow integration and experienced engineers. Autonomous agents still fail most end-to-end benchmark tasks, and evidence of lasting resilience is thin. Half the primary studies come from one hyperscale provider and none from a regulated sector, so regulated, multi-vendor enterprises should apply the results with care. The paper compares existing AIOps frameworks and proposes a governance-centered framework in which oversight shapes every stage, from data foundations to resilience. A risk-tiered adoption model separates controls backed by the reviewed studies from those drawn from ITSM, security and AI-governance standards, and a research agenda calls for outcome-level, cross-industry evaluation. The central argument is that AI’s value in ITSM rests less on model accuracy than on human oversight, grounded knowledge and an organization ready to govern it.

items.title: AI-driven urban well-being: a conceptual framework for human-centered smart cities and sustainable livability
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to inform urban planning. Machine learning and other AI methods can process data from sources like urban sensors and street-level imagery to support city monitoring and guide planning decisions. Urban planning has traditionally focused on infrastructure and operational performance, with giving less attention to social inclusion, psychological well-being, and urban equity. AI adoption is often based on technological advancements without a systematic approach towards sustainable and livable cities. This leaves a critical gap in how AI can contribute to making cities more resilient, inclusive and adaptive to environmental changes. This paper presents a conceptual framework for AI-driven urban well-being that analyzes the role of AI in public space optimization, sustainable mobility, green infrastructure, and digital governance. In this study, the connections between AI usage in urban planning and people’s well-being have been examined through systematic literature review in accordance with the guidelines for PRISMA 2020. In addition, this research includes a thematic synthesis that uses 34 peer-reviewed articles. The data from this process has been coded with the help of the application fields and with the help of the subcodes created in the process of extraction. Reviewed literature shows that AI can be used for urban monitoring, alternatives for planning modeling, and summarizing the public's views. However, evidence that acting on these outputs improves post-implementation resident outcomes or outperforms conventional planning methods remains limited. The proposed model gives policy suggestions, connects the output of AI to planning decisions/services changes, indicators of measuring residents' outcomes regardless of their demographic characteristics, and feedback mechanisms that help make further decisions. The research scope was limited to scientific publications in English language available on the Scopus and Web of Science databases. No risk of bias evaluation was conducted formally. As the framework was not validated empirically, its testing in practical planning settings is needed.

items.title: AI-POWERED PERSONALIZED LEARNING: OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES FOR STUDENT-CENTRED HIGHER EDUCATION
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping higher education by enabling learning environments that can respond more effectively to the diverse needs, abilities, preferences, and learning progress of individual students. Among these developments, AI-powered personalized learning has emerged as a significant approach for moving beyond conventional one-size-fits-all models towards more flexible and student-centred education. By using intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning platforms, learning analytics, recommendation systems, and Generative AI, higher education institutions can potentially provide individualized learning pathways, real-time feedback, targeted academic support, and learning resources suited to students’ varying levels of knowledge and achievement. This paper examines the opportunities and challenges associated with AI-powered personalized learning and considers its implications for the development of student-centred higher education. The study adopts a conceptual and analytical approach to explore how AI technologies can support adaptive instruction, learner autonomy, continuous assessment, timely feedback, early identification of learning difficulties, and inclusive educational practices. AI-supported systems can analyse patterns of student interaction and performance to recommend appropriate content, activities, and interventions. Such personalization has the potential to improve student engagement, motivation, academic performance, and self-directed learning while enabling teachers to make more informed pedagogical decisions. The paper particularly emphasises that AI should function as an educational support mechanism rather than as a replacement for teachers, whose professional judgement, empathy, contextual understanding, and human interaction remain fundamental to meaningful education. At the same time, the implementation of AI-powered personalized learning presents significant challenges concerning data privacy, algorithmic bias, transparency, digital inequality, technological dependency, academic integrity, teacher preparedness, and the ethical use of student data. Excessive dependence on automated systems may also reduce meaningful teacher–student interaction and limit opportunities for collaborative and socially situated learning. Furthermore, unequal access to technological infrastructure and differences in digital literacy may intensify existing educational inequalities. The paper therefore proposes a human-centred approach to AI-enabled personalization based on five interconnected principles: learner agency, responsible use of data, equitable access, teacher–AI collaboration, and continuous pedagogical evaluation. It argues that successful personalized learning requires an appropriate balance between technological innovation and human educational values. Higher education institutions should consequently develop clear AI policies, strengthen AI and digital literacy among teachers and students, ensure transparent and ethical data practices, and evaluate AI systems according to their contribution to genuine learning outcomes. The paper concludes that AI-powered personalized learning can contribute significantly to the transformation of higher education when personalization is understood not simply as technological automation but as a means of creating more responsive, inclusive, flexible, and learner-centred educational experiences. Responsible integration of AI can strengthen student autonomy and academic success while preserving the essential human dimensions of teaching, learning, creativity, critical thinking, and educational relationships.

items.title: AI, Automation Bias, And The Defence Of Clausewitzian Command Judgement
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into strategic command reconstitutes rather than augments command judgement, placing systematic pressure on what Clausewitz identified as the essential intelligence of command: coup d’œil, the cultivated capacity for rapid holistic synthesis that distinguishes the formed commander from the competent administrator. This article argues that command intuition develops through practice and is sustained through experience, yet three compounding pathologies in AI-augmented environments progressively erode its development and exercise. Drawing on Clausewitz’s analytical framework, the article identifies these pathologies as automation bias, which substitutes deference for judgement; algorithmic monoculture, which collapses cognitive diversity through which actors recognise what shared models cannot perceive; and delegated infopolitik, which embeds consequential political choices within system architecture, rendering them invisible to commanders and severing the accountability chain that war as an act of policy requires.

items.title: An organizational GenAI status assessment: development and first field application in Switzerland
items.abstract: Organizations need practical procedures for assessing the productive use of generative artificial intelligence, even when, like many small and medium-sized enterprises, they lack specialized AI expertise. Existing adoption and readiness models identify numerous relevant factors but offer individual firms only limited support in diagnosing their own starting position. This study therefore develops and evaluates the GenAI Status Assessment (AISA), a compact screening instrument for assessing GenAI status based on a domain model of organizational AI adoption. The instrument covers nine clusters, which are grouped into the three dimensions of the technology–organization–environment (TOE) framework. Following design science research, development proceeded in four build-evaluate cycles with expert feedback. During development, the instrument was evaluated in a case-linked manner in ten firms by comparing questionnaire responses with double-coded interview statements from the same firms. Of 106 classifiable directional comparisons of interview statements and questionnaire responses, 56 agreed in direction, in 47 at least one source showed no clear direction, and three diverged. Finally, the instrument was applied in a field study with 67 Swiss firms. After Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the nine cluster-level tests, six of the nine cluster scores correlated positively with self-reported GenAI usage stages. The strongest associations were shown by People, Processes, Market, Leadership and Usability. Trust, Leadership, Processes, and Market remained associated even after excluding items that refer to or presuppose use. The results provide initial evidence that the instrument can serve as a screening and orientation instrument that makes organizational strengths and gaps visible in a structured way.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence and Sustainable Road Safety Governance in SADC: An Ecosystem Strategy for Advancing Agenda 2063, NDP 2030 and the SDGs
items.abstract: Road traffic injuries remain a major public health, governance, and sustainable development challenge across the Southern African Development Community (SADC). Despite regional efforts to improve transportation safety and institutional effectiveness, many member states continue to experience high road traffic fatality rates, fragmented governance systems, and limited enforcement capacity. While advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and intelligent transportation systems offer new opportunities to improve road safety, existing research has focused largely on technical performance, with limited attention to ecosystem and strategic governance dimensions in developing-country contexts. This study systematically reviews the literature on AI, road safety governance, traffic policing, and smart mobility to examine how AI may support the development of sustainable smart mobility ecosystems in SADC. Guided by the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) framework, 127 studies published between 2015 and 2025 were analysed. The findings indicate that AI enhances evidence-based traffic management, predictive risk assessment, intelligent enforcement, mobility optimisation, and institutional decision-making. Beyond operational improvements, AI serves as an ecosystem enabler, supporting collaboration among transport authorities, law-enforcement agencies, municipalities, technology providers, emergency services, and citizens. However, implementation is constrained by governance weaknesses, limited institutional capacity, accountability concerns, privacy risks, algorithmic bias, and public trust deficits. The study proposes an AI-Enabled Sustainable Smart Mobility Ecosystem Framework for SADC that integrates digital intelligence, collaborative governance, institutional capacity, and sustainability objectives. The framework contributes to ecosystem strategy, smart mobility governance, and sustainable development scholarship while providing policy guidance for AI-enabled road safety governance in Africa.

items.title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE APPLICATION IN ARCHITECTURAL RENDERING: STUDENTS' ADOPTION. PERCEIVED EFFECTIVENESS AND IMPLICATIONS FOR CURRICULUM PLANNING
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing how architectural images are produced, yet most architecture schools have not decided how to teach, assess, or govern it. Existing studies mainly report single-classroom interventions and say little about how students learn AI rendering on their own or what they understand the rules to be. This study examines how architecture students adopt, learn, and evaluate AI rendering tools to inform curriculum planning. The research objectives are to describe tool use and intensity, determine whether skills stem from formal or informal learning, assess perceived effectiveness and design-intent accuracy, compare students by program, year of study, and usage intensity, and derive implications for academic integrity, design authorship, and assessment policy. Undergraduate and postgraduate architecture students at the International Islamic University Malaysia completed a cross-sectional online questionnaire. The data were analyzed with descriptive statistics, reliability testing, and nonparametric inferential tests. Most students use AI lightly, mainly through general-purpose assistants. They learned mostly through informal trial and error; very few received formal training, and many are unsure whether AI use is permitted. Students value AI for speed and visualization but are less confident that it captures their design intent. Heavier users of AI rendering applications report stronger skills and greater perceived benefit. Meanwhile, postgraduate students are more confident in their venture and more optimistic about the future than undergraduate students. The study provides early evidence from Malaysian architectural education linking student practice to policy decisions on literacy teaching and assessment, and it moves the discussion beyond technology adoption toward built-environment education. In conclusion, pedagogical programs should clearly state what AI use is allowed, teach AI literacy in stages, and assess design intent and authorship through evidence of process, because informal learning alone leaves students unsure of the rules and the accuracy of their work.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Criticality: From Recursive Self-Improvement to the Limits of Human Governance
items.abstract: English The growing automation of AI research and development has revived an old question: can systems that contribute to the design of their successors trigger a self-sustaining dynamic? Recent work formalises this dynamic as a criticality phenomenon characterised by a recursive reproduction number. This working paper addresses a related but distinct question: under what conditions could the human and institutional capacity to understand, monitor, steer and halt AI development deteriorate independently of the recursive stability regime of the R&D system? Recursive criticality and full autonomy are not treated as synonyms: high operational closure can coexist with substantial human participation, and rapid progress does not imply recursive amplification. The paper distinguishes recursive criticality, governability and institutional criticality, the latter defined as a hypothetical regime. It decomposes control into four forms (technical, cognitive, institutional and political), examines their conjunctive structure and their possible asymmetric erosion, and sets out a matrix of four hypothetical regimes. It proposes two exploratory time ratios, relating intervention time to the pace of change and to the window within which an intervention remains effective. It clarifies the heuristic use of the nuclear analogy and examines the framework against the EU Artificial Intelligence Act as amended by Regulation (EU) 2026/1744. The contribution is conceptual and integrative. It builds on recent work whose contributions it identifies (Burtsev, 2026; Lerer, 2026; Rosenbacke et al., 2026; Chan, Padarath et al., 2026; Kleiner, 2026; Kim, 2026; Doyle, Cave and Webb, 2026). It brings them together in a framework that links recursive dynamics to governability, distinguishes four forms of control, formalises the effectiveness window of an intervention and applies the whole to EU law. It draws one analytical consequence: an indicator of technical dynamics and an indicator of intervention delays are not interchangeable. It offers neither measurements nor probabilities and does not argue that an intelligence explosion is imminent. The empirical evidence used is largely self-reported by developers, and the hypotheses put forward have not been tested. Résumé — Français L’automatisation croissante de la recherche et développement (R&D) en intelligence artificielle (IA) relance une question ancienne : des systèmes capables de contribuer à la conception de leurs successeurs peuvent-ils enclencher une dynamique qui s’auto-entretient ? Des travaux récents formalisent cette dynamique comme un phénomène de criticité, caractérisé par un nombre de reproduction récursif. Ce working paper porte sur une question voisine mais distincte : dans quelles conditions la capacité humaine et institutionnelle de comprendre, surveiller, orienter et interrompre le développement de l’IA pourrait-elle se dégrader indépendamment du régime de stabilité récursive du système de R&D ? Criticité récursive et autonomie complète ne sont pas traitées comme synonymes : une fermeture opérationnelle élevée peut coexister avec une participation humaine substantielle, et une progression rapide n’implique pas une amplification récursive. Le texte distingue la criticité récursive, la gouvernabilité et la criticité institutionnelle, cette dernière étant définie comme un régime hypothétique. Il décompose le contrôle en quatre formes (technique, cognitive, institutionnelle et politique), dont il examine la structure conjonctive et la possible dégradation asymétrique. Il propose une matrice de quatre régimes hypothétiques et deux ratios temporels exploratoires, l’un rapportant le délai d’intervention au rythme d’évolution, l’autre à la fenêtre d’efficacité d’une intervention. Il précise l’usage heuristique de l’analogie nucléaire et confronte le cadre au règlement européen sur l’IA, tel que modifié par le règlement (UE) 2026/1744. La contribution est conceptuelle et intégratrice. Elle s’appuie sur des travaux récents dont elle identifie les apports (Burtsev, 2026 ; Lerer, 2026 ; Rosenbacke et al., 2026 ; Chan, Padarath et al., 2026 ; Kleiner, 2026 ; Kim, 2026 ; Doyle, Cave et Webb, 2026). Elle les articule en un cadre qui relie la dynamique récursive à la gouvernabilité, distingue quatre formes de contrôle, formalise la fenêtre d’efficacité d’une intervention et applique l’ensemble au droit de l’Union. Elle en tire une conséquence analytique : un indicateur de dynamique technique et un indicateur de délais d’intervention ne sont pas substituables. Le texte ne fournit ni mesure ni probabilité et ne soutient pas qu’une explosion d’intelligence soit imminente. Les données empiriques mobilisées sont pour l’essentiel déclaratives et proviennent des développeurs eux-mêmes ; les hypothèses formulées n’ont pas été testées.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence for Building Energy Flexibility and Grid Services: A Scoping Review with Digital Twin Perspectives
items.abstract: Buildings can support electricity-grid services through flexible energy use, but dependable delivery requires more than efficient local scheduling. This scoping review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) methods and digital twins (DTs) contribute to the prediction, control, coordination and verification of building energy flexibility. A focused title-based search of five databases identified 164 eligible primary publications through 23 August 2026; their functions, methods, building scales and evaluation settings were charted and compared, with reporting informed by PRISMA-ScR. Demand-response control and scheduling appear in 115 publications (70.1%), whereas aggregation and explicit grid services each appear in 12 (7.3%). Learning-based prediction and control dominate the evidence, while four primary publications explicitly use DTs, mainly for model-based representation, training or integration. The synthesis distinguishes the improvement of local building operation from evidence that a feasible response can be coordinated and delivered against an external request. A service-oriented framework connects assets and participants, data, models, control, coordination and grid services, with governance and lifecycle evaluation as cross-cutting considerations. It identifies interfaces and validation questions that can guide the design and assessment of dependable building flexibility services.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Accounting: Perceived Enablers and Barriers to Adoption – Evidence from Bangladesh
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and automation are changing the nature of accounting work. However, few insights explain the factors that separate professionals who report adoption from those who do not in developing economies. This paper examines how perceived technological readiness, organizational support, perceived usefulness, strategic approaches, and perceived barriers relate to respondents' reported adoption of AI and automation in accounting in Bangladesh. Using a subsample of respondents from a cross-sectional survey of 241 accounting- and finance-related professionals recruited via purposive, network-based sampling (260 questionnaires issued), the study employs a conceptual framework that selectively adapts the Technology Acceptance Model and considers the technological and organizational forces within the Technology-Organization-Environment paradigm. Confirmatory factor analysis supported the six-construct measurement model (CFI = 0.996, RMSEA = 0.012, SRMR = 0.040); composite reliabilities ranged from 0.83 to 0.88, and all heterotrait-monotrait ratios were below 0.62. The six independent variables explained 53.0% of the variance in adoption in the multiple regression models (adjusted R² = 0.520). Adoption was positively related to organizational support (β = 0.258), perceived usefulness (β = 0.257), technological readiness (β = 0.175), and strategic approaches (β = 0.174), and negatively related to perceived barriers (β = 0.214). The relative-weight analysis found no overriding importance for any predictor, and the results remained stable under heteroscedasticity-consistent errors, bootstrapping, and respondent-level controls. The evidence is predictive given the cross-sectional nature of the data and the use of non-probability, self-report data. The results can inform understanding of the context-specific digital transformation of a professional occupation in a developing economy and help establish priorities for relevant key stakeholders.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Environmental Auditing: Detecting Greenwashing, Strengthening ESG Assurance, and Improving Corporate Environmental Transparency
items.abstract: This study develops an integrated conceptual framework explaining how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen environmental auditing and corporate environmental accountability through three mechanisms: greenwashing detection, environmental, social, and governance (ESG) assurance quality, and corporate environmental transparency. The study employs an integrative literature review and theory-driven conceptual synthesis, drawing on legitimacy theory, agency theory, stakeholder theory, and information-asymmetry theory. The synthesis examines the potential contributions of AI-enabled environmental auditing and develops three theoretical propositions concerning its accountability mechanisms and enabling conditions. The framework identifies three interconnected mechanisms. First, AI may improve greenwashing detection by identifying discrepancies between environmental claims and supporting evidence. Second, AI may strengthen ESG assurance quality through evidence evaluation, data reconciliation, and inconsistency detection. Third, AI may enhance environmental transparency by improving information traceability, consistency, and verifiability. These mechanisms may collectively strengthen corporate environmental accountability. Their effectiveness depends on five enabling conditions: environmental data quality and integration, model explainability and audit-trail documentation, executive oversight and organizational governance, auditor independence and professional judgment, and regulatory requirements and external monitoring. The study integrates three environmental-accountability mechanisms and five enabling conditions into a unified conceptual framework. It offers theoretically grounded propositions for empirical testing while clarifying that AI complements, rather than replaces, professional auditing judgment.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Delivery at South African Public Clinics: A Desktop Review
items.abstract: This study examines the impact of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on healthcare delivery in South African public clinics, with particular attention to the extent of current adoption, the barriers and enablers that shape implementation, and the recommendations emerging from the existing literature. It also examines whether the documented benefits of AI in this context are matched by the regulatory, infrastructural, and governance structures needed to sustain them. A desktop review was conducted using thematic analysis of six selected sources published in 2025, comprising five journal publications and one institutional roundtable source. The sources were analysed based on their treatment of AI applications, benefits, barriers, enabling conditions, and recommendations relevant to healthcare delivery, with particular attention to South African evidence. The reviewed literature suggests that AI adoption in South African public healthcare is occurring through promising but isolated case studies, such as tuberculosis screening and breast-cancer detection tools, rather than through facility-wide integration. Four recurring barriers constrain implementation: infrastructure constraints, regulatory and governance gaps, data privacy concerns, and skills shortages rooted in structural inequity. Proactive regulatory leadership, workforce development, interoperable digital infrastructure, and human-in-the-loop governance emerge as important enablers. Recommendations converge on the need for healthcare-specific AI governance, secure and interoperable health-information systems, workforce training, and phased, equity-focused implementation beginning in under-resourced clinics. The study concludes that South African discourse on AI in healthcare contains two related strands: one documenting isolated successes and another explaining why these successes have not yet scaled. Future progress depends on addressing both strands together

items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Higher Education: Opportunities, Challenges and Responsible Practice
items.abstract: This study note explores the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education, focusing on its opportunities, challenges, and responsible use in academic environments. It discusses how AI technologies can support teaching, learning, research, content creation, problem-solving, and student development. The document highlights the potential benefits of AI-assisted learning while examining important concerns such as information accuracy, algorithmic bias, data privacy, cybersecurity, and academic integrity. It also provides practical guidelines for students to evaluate AI-generated content, use AI tools responsibly, and maintain transparency in academic work. Additionally, this study note includes a four-week learning plan and a self-assessment checklist to help undergraduate students develop AI literacy and responsible digital learning practices.

items.title: Artificial intelligence in L2 listening education: a comparative-critical review of ethical challenges and pedagogical opportunities
items.abstract: This comparative review synthesizes 45 empirical studies published between January 2016 and March 2025 to critically examine the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into L2 listening instruction, including speech recognition tools, text-to-speech systems, intelligent tutoring platforms, chatbots, and emerging VR/AR environments. Guided by PRISMA 2020, the review uses systematic screening, dual-coder data extraction (κ = 0.88), and MMAT appraisal to strengthen methodological transparency. Findings suggest that AI-supported environments are often associated with gains in bottom-up listening processes, including phonemic discrimination, segmentation, and decoding, while also supporting learner engagement, personalized pacing, and reduced processing demands, particularly among lower-proficiency learners. Recurrent limitations include algorithmic bias, over-scaffolding, multimodal cognitive overload, data-privacy vulnerabilities, and diminished socio-pragmatic authenticity. Although several studies reported advantages of AI-enhanced environments for precision-oriented micro-skill development, teacher-mediated approaches remain important for higher-order comprehension, cultural nuance, and interactional competence. Overall, the evidence supports conceptualizing AI as a pedagogical enhancer rather than a replacement for human instruction and highlights the need for longitudinal research, culturally diverse datasets, transparent governance, and ethically grounded integration.

items.title: Artificial intelligence reliance and the psychological safety of researchers: the moderating role of ethical determinants
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in scientific research necessitates robust institutional governance; however, empirical frameworks evaluating its psychological outcomes among researchers remain limited. Grounded in Sociotechnical Systems Theory, Self-Determination Theory, and Ethical Climate Theory, this study evaluated the impact of artificial intelligence reliance (AIR) on researchers’ psychological safety (PS) in Yemeni universities, while examining the moderating role of ethical determinants (ED). Utilizing a cross-sectional design, data were collected from 500 active researchers and graduate students across public and private universities via an online survey using a purposive sampling approach and analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). Descriptive results indicated low baseline levels across AIR, ED, and PS, reflecting a prevailing regulatory vacuum. The structural model revealed a non-significant direct effect of AIR on psychological safety, indicating that technological reliance alone does not act as a direct determinant of scholarly well-being. Conversely, ED exerted a significant positive direct effect on psychological safety. Crucially, ED significantly moderated the AIR–PS relationship: under low ethical governance, increased AIR was associated with diminished psychological safety and heightened compliance anxiety, whereas under robust ethical frameworks, this negative pattern was mitigated, reinforcing psychological safety even under high AIR usage. Theoretically, this study clarifies the boundary conditions governing human-AI interaction in academia. Practically, it highlights the need for higher education leaders to establish transparent ethical policies and disclosure norms that mitigate evaluative ambiguity and support scholarly well-being.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Use, Workload, Productivity, and Job Satisfaction Among Lecturers in Phnom Penh Universities
items.abstract: Universities are adopting artificial intelligence (AI) for teaching, assessment, research, and administration, yet little is known about how this adoption relates to the work experience of lecturers. This study examined the associations between AI use and lecturers' workload, productivity, and job satisfaction at five universities in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. A quantitative survey was conducted with 385 lecturers, drawn through an equal quota of 77 participants per university, using a questionnaire with 5-point Likert items. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach's alpha, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression were applied. Lecturers rated all dimensions highly, with mean scores from 4.00 to 4.40. Greater AI use was positively associated with perceived workload and productivity, which supported the first two hypotheses, and with job satisfaction. Workload was also positively associated with job satisfaction, which did not support the expected negative relationship, while the mediation hypotheses were not tested. Correlation, regression, and reliability coefficients approached or reached 1.000, which pointed to overlap among the composite scores, so only the direction of the relationships was interpreted. The results suggest that AI use accompanies both higher productivity and higher perceived workload, and they do not show that AI simply reduces the burden on lecturers. Institutions should therefore pair AI adoption with clear protocols, training, and support, and future studies should verify the data and test mediation.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence, Ethical Use and Academic Integrity in South African Higher Education: Perspectives of University Students
items.abstract: This study examines the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) on academic integrity among university students in South Africa. AI tools increasingly assist students with academic writing, idea development, and content generation, raising new ethical questions for higher education as institutions grapple with limited guidance on responsible use. The study was guided by the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), which explains technology adoption through perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use. A qualitative case study design was adopted, involving semi-structured interviews with 12 undergraduate students, analysed using Braun and Clarke's (2006) six-step thematic analysis. Findings show that students value AI for improving academic writing and efficiency, yet experience uncertainty about ethical boundaries in the absence of clear and consistently communicated institutional policy, and worry that unreflective use may erode critical thinking and originality. The study concludes that AI is neither inherently beneficial nor harmful to academic integrity, and its effect depends on how institutions govern its use and how students exercise judgment in applying it. The study recommends that universities develop comprehensive AI policies, integrate AI ethics and digital literacy into the curriculum, and redesign assessment practices to promote critical thinking, originality, and responsible AI use.

items.title: Attitudes and anxiety toward artificial intelligence among healthcare professionals and students: a systematic review
items.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) is a major technological advancement in healthcare, often viewed favourably, although concerns persist. This systematic review aimed to synthesise the available evidence on attitudes toward artificial intelligence (AI) and AI-related anxiety among healthcare professionals and healthcare students. Methods This study was performed according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, and the protocol was registered with PROSPERO (CRD420261286794). Two authors independently searched five electronic databases (PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Embase) using combinations of MeSH terms and keywords for artificial intelligence, the target population, and the attitude/anxiety outcomes, for descriptive/cross-sectional or observational research articles published from 1 January 2016 to 31 January 2026. Methodological quality was assessed using the JBI critical appraisal checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies. Results From 146 records identified, 44 cross-sectional studies (28,452 participants) from 19 countries, predominantly Türkiye and Middle Eastern nations, met the inclusion criteria: 36 assessed attitude only, seven assessed anxiety only, and one assessed both attitude and anxiety. Many studies reported favourable attitudes toward AI, although findings varied across populations and measurement instruments. AI-related anxiety, evidenced only in Turkish samples, followed identifiable patterns rather than a generalised fear. Male gender was associated with more favourable attitudes in five studies, while one reported the opposite. Prior AI training or knowledge was linked to more favourable attitudes or lower anxiety in only a few studies, and findings for age and seniority were mixed. Individual study sample sizes ranged from 107 to 4492. Conclusion Many studies of healthcare professionals and students reported favourable attitudes toward AI, although the evidence rests largely on self-developed instruments and is best read as a qualitative summary rather than a pooled estimate. AI-related anxiety, documented only among Turkish samples, was associated in some studies with age, gender, prior training, and knowledge regarding AI. These findings reflect associations rather than causal effects, given the cross-sectional design. Because most attitude studies used self-developed rather than validated instruments, further quantitative synthesis using comparable, validated tools is warranted.

items.title: Barriers to Artificial Intelligence Integration in Social Media Intelligence (SOCMINT): Evidence from South African Retail Organisations
items.abstract: Although artificial intelligence (AI) has become a critical enabler of advanced social media intelligence (SOCMINT), its adoption remains uneven across industries, particularly in emerging markets. This study investigates the organisational, technical and capability-related barriers that limit AI integration within SOCMINT practices in South Africa’s retail sector. Using quantitative data from 344 managers across multiple retail categories, the study reveals exceptionally low levels of AI utilization across all SOCMINT phases, including data collection, sorting, analysis and dissemination. Despite high agreement that SOCMINT improves decision-making, respondents indicated minimal ability to automate intelligence processes, set AI instructions or use AI-generated outputs in decision-making. The findings highlight significant gaps in digital maturity, analytical skills, data governance readiness and technological infrastructure. These constraints are further exacerbated by hesitancy towards cloud-based systems, reliance on manual tools and a lack of organisational strategic commitment to AI-driven intelligence. The study contributes to growing debates on digital transformation by presenting an empirically and theoretically grounded SOCMINT AI readiness framework for South African retail organisations. Practical implications include a need for structured capability development, investment in cross-platform analytics tools, and the establishment of AI-governed intelligence workflows. Recommendations for policy, managerial training and future research are provided.

items.title: Basic concepts, research, and commercialization of medical artificial intelligence in Korea: a narrative review
items.abstract: Purpose: Although artificial intelligence is now a familiar term, physicians still find it difficult to determine whether a particular product will benefit their patients. This review explains the concepts needed to make that judgment and describes software approved in Korea.Current concepts: Machine learning, foundation models, and large language models are often treated as interchangeable terms, although each raises different questions about what requires testing. Accuracy should be assessed in three ways. A model should distinguish patients with disease from those without it, its predicted risk should agree with observed risk, and its use should provide more benefit than harm. The area under the receiver operating characteristic curve is unaffected by disease prevalence, whereas positive predictive value falls sharply when disease is rare. Validation progresses through stages involving new data, silent use, prospective care, and a randomized trial.Discussion and conclusion: Approvals and certifications in Korea increased from 37 in 2021 to 153 in 2025. Korean groups have conducted randomized or prospective trials in electrocardiography, coronary intervention, chest radiography, mammography, colonoscopy, dermatology, and ward monitoring. These tools increased lung nodule detection during screening, adenoma detection during colonoscopy, and breast cancer detection without increasing recalls. As artificial intelligence improves, clinical questions become more specific: where to use a tool, whether it changes care, and when to discontinue its use. Answering these questions requires clinicians who understand their patients and clinical settings; their judgment becomes increasingly important as these tools are more widely adopted.

items.title: BEYOND AUTOMATION: A CANDIDATE-CENTRED FRAMEWORK FOR RESPONSIBLE ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE I RECRUITMENT – INTEGRATING FAIRNESS, TRANSPARENCY, TRUST AND HUMAN OVERSIGHT
items.abstract: The growing use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in recruitment is changing how employers identify, assess and select prospective employees. AI applications can process large applicant pools, support résumé screening and assist with preliminary assessments. At the same time, their use raises questions about unequal treatment, the explainability of decisions, the handling of personal information and the extent to which applicants can rely on automated recommendations. This paper develops a candidate-centred conceptual framework for the responsible use of AI in recruitment. Informed by organisational justice theory, trust in automation and responsible AI principles, the framework brings together five governance dimensions: algorithmic fairness, decision transparency, responsible data practices, meaningful human oversight, and candidate participation with access to redress. It proposes that these practices shape applicants’ perceptions of recruitment justice and trust, which may subsequently influence their willingness to accept AI-assisted recruitment. Organisational accountability and continuous monitoring are presented as cross-cutting conditions that support the effective implementation of the five dimensions. The paper contributes to HRM thinking by moving the discussion beyond operational efficiency and placing candidate experience, ethical safeguards and organisational responsibility at the centre of AI-enabled recruitment. Implications for HR practitioners and directions for future empirical investigation are also outlined.

items.title: Chain-of-thought LLMs provide complementary critical thinking assessments on problem-posing tasks in Latin America
items.abstract: Critical thinking is essential for addressing complex societal challenges and involves not only solving problems but also formulating them. Problem posing is particularly demanding because it requires deeper understanding, creativity, and the ability to construct coherent chains of reasoning. Yet, evaluating such creative outputs is complex and time-consuming. This study examines LLM-supported assessment of deductive “lost-object” problem posing among 154 students, pre-service teachers, and in-service teachers from three Latin American countries. Clarity and creativity were evaluated by two human raters and two GPT-5.5 configurations: zero-shot and four-shot prompting. Both algorithmic, dimension-by-dimension scoring and holistic evaluation strategies were employed. Human–LLM assessments showed moderate agreement, suggesting that LLMs can provide detailed complementary analyses, although they do not fully reproduce human judgments. According to the results, 79.66% of students, 67.74% of pre-service teachers, and 58.82% of in-service teachers correctly solved the initial problem, indicating broadly comparable capabilities across groups. However, constructing a new, valid deductive problem requiring multiple logically interconnected necessary clues proved substantially more challenging. Only 4.0%–10.1% of submissions received the maximum score of six necessary clues, depending on the evaluator. This gap highlights the distinction between solving a CoT problem and creatively formulating one requiring an extended chain of reasoning. LLM-supported assessment offers a promising, scalable resource for teachers to examine these higher-order reasoning processes.

items.title: Challenges, Strategies, and Future Directions of AI-Assisted Clinical Decision-Making Systems for Oncology Diagnosis and Treatment
items.abstract: Oncology diagnosis and treatment is undergoing a profound transformation from empirical medicine to data-driven precision medicine. With its pattern recognition advantages in high-dimensional heterogeneous data, artificial intelligence has become a key technological driver of this transformation. However, from laboratory performance verification to real-world implementation of clinical decision support systems, AI models still face multiple systemic obstacles such as the contradiction between model opacity and fault tolerance system integration barriers, data silo effect and rigid constraints of privacy protection. Taking this as the main line of logic, this article first analyzes the intrinsic relationship of the above challenges: Opacity erodes clinical trust, fault tolerance requirements and diagnosis and treatment safety form tension, and the bottlenecks at the data and infrastructure levels further amplify the algorithm risk. Then, put forward a targeted solution strategy: develop an AI model based on the fine-tuning of disease-specific knowledge, so that the general-purpose foundation model can internalize evidence-based logic and implicit decision-making experience, so as to bridge the interpretability gap while improving professional reliability; Promote the intelligent decision-making architecture of the native integration of multi-modal data, approach the panoramic cognition of tumors through cross-modal collaborative interaction, and realize the synergistic gain of accuracy and interpretation. Looking forward to the future, with reliable infrastructure, continuous learning and full lifecycle governance as the core direction, we emphasize that only by attaching the same importance to technological innovation and institutional evolution can AI become a reliable intelligent partner for multidisciplinary oncology teams and truly serve patient-centered precision medicine goals.

items.title: Competencies shaping the use of AI-based assistive technology among people with visual impairments: content domains and priorities
items.abstract: This study explored the content domains of artificial intelligence (AI) literacy relevant to people with visual impairments (VIs) and the priorities assigned to these competencies by different stakeholder groups. Eight experts in VI reviewed the content validity of items identified through purposive literature sampling. The review identified 53 items across eight domains. 82 stakeholders rated item importance using essentiality endorsement proportion/ratio (EP/ER). Priorities were examined using the top-priority selections of 53 stakeholders (64.6%). Open-ended responses were analysed thematically and integrated with quantitative findings using a joint display. All 42 original items were retained, and 11 items were added during the expert review. All items exceeded the reference criterion for ER (>0.195), whereas two items related to creation had EP values below 0.78. The most frequently selected priorities were recognising potential errors in AI explanations (0.547) and using AI to read printed materials (0.472). Priorities are dispersed within the groups (Kendall’s W = 0.12, 0.09), and no items differed significantly between groups. Open-ended responses additionally identified prerequisite assistive technology competencies, prompts that specify disability context, nonvisual recording, and institutional support. The findings highlight information access and use, AI tool accessibility, output verification, and self-advocacy as specialised AI literacy domains for people with VI. The framework highlights the need to account for the distinct access requirements of people with VI. Profile-based training, appropriate educational infrastructure, and accessibility verification systems are needed to accommodate differences in visual impairment and primary access media. For users with blindness and low vision, artificial intelligence (AI) tools constitute a form of assistive technology (AT), and user competencies determine their adoption, effective use, and abandonment. Proficiency in operating screen readers and digital devices should be assessed as a prerequisite for AI use and addressed early in the AT service delivery process, rather than treated solely as a criterion for selecting suitable tools. Nonvisual verification of AI outputs and prior assessment of tool accessibility are directly related to safety but are not specified in general AI literacy frameworks and should therefore be explicitly addressed in rehabilitation training. Priorities vary according to the degree of visual impairment and primary access medium; therefore, training should follow user profiles rather than a single standardised sequence. items.title: Complex analyses for complex problems: Beyond the pathologization of Generative AI and the stigmatization of its use
items.abstract: Is the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) going to degrade management knowledge? In their point essay, Nolan, Lindebaum, and Ashraf (2026) (NLA hereafter) argue that LLMs will unavoidably degrade knowledge production in management and organization studies—eroding deep reading, dissuading scholars from the real world, diminishing collegial engagement, and homogenizing scholarly output. In our counterpoint essay, we argue that this dire diagnosis undeservedly pathologizes a technology for the problems created by systemic shortcomings that predate its advent, and it erroneously infers the degradation of knowledge from individual misuse since the corpus of knowledge is decided by system-level factors. Rather than stigmatizing the use of LLMs, we maintain that our focus should be on addressing preexisting pathologies that the technology is only making more pressing—chiefly about the effectiveness of our filtering systems. We also show that in capturing only reinforcing loops, NLA’s deterministic model fails to acknowledge (1) the positive dynamics associated with the productive use of the technology and (2) the balancing dynamics of second-order effects—scarcity premiums and sharpened gatekeeping. Finally, we challenge widespread philosophical assumptions underpinning NLA’s anti-LLM skepticism, explaining that they rest on the reification of meaning and an anthropomorphic conception of intelligence.

items.title: Current perspectives and review of artificial intelligence solutions in cancer management: a narrative review
items.abstract: Purpose: Advances in deep learning and graphics processing unit-based computing, together with the growth of digital clinical data, have expanded the medical applications of artificial intelligence (AI). This review examines the performance and clinical evidence for selected AI tools across cancer diagnosis, treatment decision-making, and patient management, emphasizing tools commercially available or authorized in Korea.Current concepts: Software authorized by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety for mammography (Lunit INSIGHT MMG), low-dose chest computed tomography (AVIEW LCS), and prostate biopsy pathology (DeepDx-Prostate) has been evaluated in a prospective cohort study, retrospective analyses, and an external validation study, respectively. These findings apply specifically to the products and software versions studied. Evidence for the digital breast tomosynthesis tool Genius AI Detection 2.0 remains limited to a retrospective analysis. For treatment planning, the knowledge-based decision support system IBM Watson for Oncology showed variable concordance with Korean multidisciplinary decisions. Multimodal AI models integrating digital pathology and clinical data showed predictive or prognostic performance in post hoc analyses of randomized trials. Electronic patient-reported outcome-based monitoring and large language models are emerging approaches to patient management, although supporting evidence remains preliminary.Discussion and conclusion: The evidence comes predominantly from retrospective or validation studies, with limited data on patient-centered outcomes and cost-effectiveness. AI should assist clinicians while preserving their clinical judgment. Widespread adoption requires external validation of individual products, ongoing performance monitoring, and prospective evaluation in real-world practice.

items.title: Decision Rights in Human–AI Organizations: A Matched Simulation of Agent Autonomy, Human Accountability, and Review Workload
items.abstract: AbstractAs AI agents acquire execution capabilities, organizations face a design problem: how to delegate routine actions without diffusing accountability or imposing unnecessary review. This paper proposes a four-tier decision-rights model and examines its operational logic in a synthetic business-workflow sandbox. Using 1,000 matched cases, it compares unrestricted decision rights, blanket human review of mutations, and risk-tiered governance combined with a trusted operation mandate. In the default simulation, the combined configuration has 0 trials with unauthorized persistent mutations, versus 268 and 5 in the alternatives, and routes 341 cases to review rather than 785 under blanket review. The corresponding numbers of unauthorized changed database records are 0, 376 and 7, respectively. A post-hoc ablation records 6 affected trials for tier rules alone and 190 for the mandate alone. Sensitivity tests reveal residual vulnerabilities under modeled reviewer error. These are executable policy comparisons conditional on investigator-designed cases, trusted mandates and oracle-based simulated reviews. They do not establish live-model safety, actual human performance, workplace productivity or enterprise readiness. Key findingsAcross 1,000 matched synthetic cases per arm, the tiered policy plus trusted operation mandate recorded 0 trials with unauthorized persistent mutations and routed 341 cases to simulated review. Unrestricted rights recorded 268 affected trials; blanket review recorded 5 and routed 785 cases to review. The combined arm produced 91.8% correct outcomes, compared with 71.7% and 89.7%. Costs and latency are model outputs under the stated assumptions, not observed operational results. Method and limitationsThe experiment uses investigator-designed synthetic cases, a seeded proposal-error process, fixed sandbox operations, and simulated reviews with fixture-defined legitimacy. Arm C combines tier-specific routing with a trusted mandate; the main comparison does not isolate the tier structure, and a post-hoc ablation records 6 affected trials for tier rules alone and 190 for the mandate alone. Sensitivity settings reuse the same task set. The results describe executable policy behavior in this sandbox; they do not test live-model safety, actual human performance, employee outcomes, productivity, or enterprise readiness. The prototype does not provide a separate authenticated human execution principal; multi-tenant isolation, distributed transactions, concurrent writes, approval expiry, real audit-sink failures, and deployment remain unvalidated. The V2 suite is a developer-authored regression suite, not independent validation. No external model calls or real human reviews were used in the supplied results. AI assistance was used substantially in developing the prototype, designing fixtures, executing computational checks, and drafting/revising the manuscript. The author approved the final claims and accepts responsibility for the work. Funding: No external funding. Competing interests: None declared. No actual employee or participant records were used. The research was initially prepared as a professional work sample; OpenAI did not commission, sponsor, or validate it.
