items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has become the most transformative technology in the 21st century. In education, AI is redefining how teachers teach and students learn. The present study titled "AI Creates New Challenges and Opportunities in Teaching and Learning" investigates the dual nature of AI in education. On one hand, AI offers personalized learning, intelligent tutoring systems (ITS), automated assessment, virtual assistants, and inclusive education through translation and accessibility tools. Platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, Khan Academy, BYJU'S and Google Bard are helping students learn at their own pace, anytime and anywhere. On the other hand, AI brings serious challenges such as academic dishonesty, over-reliance on technology, data privacy risks, lack of teacher training, digital divide between rural and urban students of Punjab, reduced human emotional connection, and the spread of misinformation through AI hallucinations. This research is based on secondary data collected from UNESCO (2023), NITI Aayog (2024), and primary feedback from 20 students of Patiala district. The findings show that 60% of students use AI tools, but only 30% teachers are formally trained. The paper concludes that AI cannot replace a human teacher but can be a powerful assistant. A balanced model of 70% human teaching + 30% AI support is recommended for sustainable and ethical education.

items.title: Designing for Meaningful Participation: Human-Centered Learning Experiences in AI-Supported Second-Language Learning
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly reshaping second-language learning by expanding learners’ access to conversational practice, personalized feedback, and interaction opportunities. However, greater access to communicative interactions does not automatically yield meaningful participation, as learners may have abundant chances to interact with AI yet remain unwilling to take risks, make errors, or express authentic ideas. This literature review explores how human-centered learning design fosters meaningful participation within AI-supported second-language learning contexts. Synthesizing scholarship on AI-enhanced education, psychological safety, learner agency, and communicative purpose, this review identifies three core prerequisites shaping learner engagement: perceived safety for communication, learner agency over the learning journey, and authentic communicative motivation. Building on this synthesis, the paper develops a conceptual framework that links AI-enabled learning environments, human-centered design principles, and meaningful learner participation. It further demonstrates that technical affordances alone cannot guarantee quality engagement; learning experiences must prioritize learners’ subjective experiences rather than technological capabilities. The review concludes by pinpointing notable gaps within current scholarship and outlining targeted directions for subsequent empirical inquiry into AI-assisted language education.

items.title: Designing REVEAL: a generative AI tool to support viewing and discussing educational videos in K–2 literacy and mathematics instruction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) in education is often designed for direct, individualized interaction with students. This article examines an alternative approach in which AI operates upstream of instruction to help teachers prepare shared learning experiences. We describe the educator-informed development of Recommending Educational Videos for Elementary Learning (REVEAL), a teacher-facing tool intended to help K–2 educators find and use publicly available videos for literacy and mathematics instruction. Formative development activities included six focus groups with 29 teachers and instructional coaches, three co-development activities with a six-member educator advisory board, and two rounds of task-based prototype testing comprising 12 sessions with 11 participants. REVEAL's initial design included personalized video recommendations, questions, and automated feedback delivered directly to individual students. Educators instead described video as primarily a shared classroom resource and redirected the design toward teacher-directed search and selection, and whole-class viewing and discussion. They prioritized education-specific filters, concise video information, teacher ratings, and adaptable questions that extend beyond recall. Prototype testing translated these priorities into concrete revisions to the search, video-detail, and discussion-support features. The resulting design uses AI to analyze and organize videos and generate possible discussion questions while leaving teachers responsible for selecting content and adapting discussion questions. The case suggests three transferable principles: begin with existing instructional routines, use AI to prepare opportunities for human interaction, and preserve educator judgment. Subject to future funding, planned work would validate REVEAL's AI-generated supports and examine its feasibility and impacts during classroom use.

items.title: Developing Human Capability in the Dual-Intelligence World
items.abstract: Developing Human Capability in the Dual-Intelligence World: Human Development, Epistemic Agency, and the Educational Responsibilities of Higher Education, by Antonia Anderson, examines the evolving responsibilities of higher education as Human Intelligence and Digital Intelligence increasingly collaborate. The monograph explores a fundamental distinction between AI-assisted task performance, genuine learning, and transferable human capability. Drawing upon research in cognitive science, educational psychology, organizational behavior, and human–AI interaction, it proposes five interconnected domains of human development: critical thinking and independent judgment; metacognition and self-regulated learning; problem identification and systems thinking; creativity and adaptability; and interpersonal understanding and ethical responsibility. Particular attention is given to epistemic agency, productive cognitive effort, experiential learning, career readiness, and the importance of maintaining meaningful Human-in-Authority in AI-supported environments. The monograph also identifies opportunities for future research into how Collaborative Intelligence can strengthen human capability rather than foster cognitive dependency. Published in the Genesis Research Monograph Series by Genesis Digital Intelligence, this work is a companion to Richard Hoffmann's Revelations in Cognitive Liberation: Discovering New Old Thinking in the Dual-Intelligence World. Together, the monographs examine complementary dimensions of Human Elevation and the emerging field of Collaborative Intelligence.

items.title: Development and initial validation of the self-reported CBRN knowledge and protective-behavior orientation scale
items.abstract: Background CBRN incidents are considered a challenge for both public health and emergency preparedness, but they also represent an occupational health problem. Awareness of the risks and an adequate response to the threats are important elements of individual preparedness. Nevertheless, there is little research on how people perceive their knowledge in terms of CBRN threats and protective behaviors. Purpose This study aimed to develop a scale assessing self-reported CBRN knowledge and protective behavior orientation among adults and to examine its initial psychometric properties. Methods This methodology-based study was carried out between February and May 2026 on adults above the age of 18 years residing in Ankara, Türkiye. The subjects for the study were selected through convenience sampling, and the data collection procedure involved administering an online questionnaire using Google forms that was spread via WhatsApp and social media platforms. Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) were used on separate samples (EFA sample n = 552 and CFA sample n = 394). Results The EFA produced a two-factor structure of 19 items (KMO = 0.958), namely “Risk and Protective Behaviors” (10 items) and “Basic Knowledge” (9 items), accounting for 77.12% of the total variance. The CFA demonstrated that the two-factor structure fit the data reasonably well (χ 2 /df = 3.49, RMSEA = 0.080, CFI = 0.98, NNFI = 0.97). Factor loadings for the Risk and Protective Behavior construct varied from 0.28 to 0.87, suggesting poor measurement for some items. Cronbach’s alpha was found to be 0.914, while McDonald’s omega was 0.926 for the overall scale. Composite reliabilities for the subscales were 0.829 and 0.919, whereas average variances extracted (AVE) amounted to 0.512 and 0.563 correspondingly. Nevertheless, the heterotrait–monotrait ratio (HTMT = 0.933) suggested lack of discriminant validity. Conclusion The Self-Reported CBRN Knowledge and Protective Behavior Orientation Scale provides initial evidence that adults’ perceived CBRN knowledge, risk awareness and protective behavior orientation can be measured. Further studies are needed to confirm its dimensionality and discriminant validity and to test its applicability across populations. Its use in occupational health and safety should be examined in occupational groups such as workplace emergency responders, healthcare professionals and hazardous materials workers.

items.title: Development and validation of a generative AI readiness scale for K-12 teachers: knowledge, beliefs, practice and the regulation of cognitive offloading
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) allows teachers to offload parts of lesson planning and material production, so using it well requires regulating what is delegated and checking what is returned. To develop the Generative AI Readiness Scale for Teachers (GAIRS-T), a pool of 47 items, written from research on AI literacy, teachers' competence and value beliefs and the metacognitive regulation of cognitive offloading, was screened through a content audit and item analysis. In a cross-sectional online survey, 284 K-12 teachers in China were recruited by convenience sampling; random halves served exploratory factor and item analyses, followed by confirmatory factor, Rasch, measurement invariance and criterion analyses. The final 18 items measure AI understanding, instructional self-efficacy, perceived educational value, instructional application, human–AI task division and critical agency. The six-factor model fitted well (CFI = 0.985, RMSEA = 0.044) and outperformed all models merging adjacent dimensions, and reliability, convergent and discriminant validity and scalar invariance across four teacher subgroups were supported. Although a general factor accounted for most total-score variance, every dimension score added reliable information beyond it, so the scale is best used as a profile of six dimension scores. Critical agency showed the strongest association with self-reported verification of AI output (r = 0.38), although its advantage over self-efficacy was small, and no dimension was more than weakly related to concern, dependence anxiety or technostress. Because the evidence comes from a single convenience sample concentrated in one province, the scale requires confirmation in independent samples.

items.title: Digital Occupational Preferences in Cambodian Higher Education and Differences by Expertise and Age
items.abstract: Digital transformation is changing the occupations that graduates can enter, yet little is known about which digital occupations Cambodian university students favor. Preference ratings for 26 digital occupations were collected from 335 respondents at BELTEI International University through a five-point questionnaire with good internal consistency (Cronbach’s alpha = .879). Means and standard deviations ranked the occupations, independent samples t tests compared gender and type of institution, and one-way analyses of variance compared major of study, area of expertise, age group, and position. All occupations were rated favorably (M = 3.81 to 4.18). Electro technology engineers, digital marketing and strategy specialists, and system engineers ranked highest, whereas FinTech engineers and artificial intelligence and machine learning specialists ranked lowest. Area of expertise differed significantly for 24 occupations, age group for 18, and major of study for 15, and 40 of the 66 significant results remained significant after a Bonferroni adjustment. Gender, type of institution, and position produced only a few small differences that did not survive the adjustment. The findings suggest that universities should differentiate digital course offerings and career counseling by professional background and age, and should expose students to the data-intensive occupations in which interest was lowest. The cross-sectional, single-institution design limits generalization, and later studies should add post hoc tests, multiple institutions, and measures of the factors behind preference.

items.title: Digital Twin for Industrial Control: High-Fidelity Mapping, Closed-Loop Optimization, and Embodied Intelligence Evolution
items.abstract: Digital twin technology is undergoing a paradigm shift from static reproduction to dynamic closed-loop control in industrial control. Following the logic of "high-fidelity mapping-state deduction-closed-loop optimization-embodied evolution", this paper systematically reviews the technical system, application paradigms, and frontier trends. It analyzes the implementation and bottlenecks of virtual-real dynamic mapping from multi-dimensional modeling, data fusion, and low-code visualization; elaborates the value of hybrid-driven state deduction in predictive maintenance and anomaly warning; reveals the closed-loop optimization mechanisms for single-equipment online tuning, multi-agent scheduling, and reinforcement-learning-based control; and proposes the enabling paradigm of digital twin as a virtual sandbox for embodied intelligence with a closed-loop evolution path. Current challenges in real-time performance, standardization, generalization, and security are summarized, and future directions including hybrid modeling, edge-cloud architecture, generative AI integration, and unified data governance are outlined. This paper provides a systematic reference and roadmap for digital twin transitioning from an auxiliary tool to an autonomous intelligent core engine.

items.title: DILEMA ETIKA DALAM AUDIT BERBASIS ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE : DISRUPSI ATAS AKUNTABILITAS DAN SKEPTISISME PROFESIONAL AUDITOR?
items.abstract: Digital transformation has driven the increased use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in audit practices, but this development has also raised various ethical issues that have not been comprehensively discussed, particularly regarding auditor accountability and professional skepticism. This research aims to analyze the ethical dilemmas that arise in AI-based audits and explain the relationship between technology use, auditor accountability, and professional skepticism through a literature review approach. The research uses the Systematic Literature Review method by analyzing various relevant scientific publications from the period 2020–2025. The literature is obtained from reputable academic databases and analyzed using a thematic approach to identify key issues that have developed in previous research. The study results show that AI contributes to improving the efficiency, effectiveness, and quality of the audit process through its ability to analyze data more quickly and comprehensively. However, the use of AI also raises ethical dilemmas such as limited algorithm transparency, potential system bias, and the risk of auditor dependence on technology analysis results (automation bias). This research found that the higher the level of AI utilization in audits, the more important the roles of accountability and professional skepticism become as control mechanisms to maintain the quality of auditor judgment. The contribution of this research lies in the formulation of a conceptual synthesis that positions AI, accountability, and professional skepticism as three interrelated elements in shaping ethical and reliable audit practices in the digital era. The research findings are expected to serve as a reference for the development of professional standards, auditor education, and technology-based audit governance policies.

items.title: Disciplinary embeddedness as a critical condition for internalising academic integrity values
items.abstract: Academic integrity remains a persistent challenge in higher education despite extensive institutional investment in policy, educational programmes, and technological detection systems. The emergence of generative artificial intelligence has intensified these challenges, exposing limitations in prevailing approaches that emphasise compliance, surveillance, and procedural instruction. While such approaches have improved awareness of integrity requirements, their effectiveness in fostering durable values internalisation remains limited. This paper argues that this limitation arises substantially from a structural condition: the separation of integrity education from the disciplinary contexts in which scholarly values acquire meaning. Drawing on self-determination theory, moral identity theory, Bourdieu’s concept of habitus, and Wenger’s communities of practice, the paper argues that disciplinary embeddedness is a critical enabling condition for the internalisation of academic integrity values in many higher education contexts. Disciplinary embeddedness connects institutional expectations to the practices, relationships, and forms of judgement through which scholarly identity develops, while acknowledging that comparable conditions may in principle be created through other sustained scholarly communities, such as clinical supervision, research mentorship, or professional practice communities. The paper positions commonly deployed student-facing mechanisms, including academic integrity modules, honour codes, and plagiarism detection tools, as complementary scaffolds rather than substitutes for curriculum-embedded disciplinary teaching, limited on their own by delivery outside disciplinary teaching relationships but retaining a legitimate role once reoriented to support rather than replace it. In response, the paper develops a values-based enculturation framework specifying five interdependent pedagogical mechanisms. These are role modelling, curriculum integration, developmental sequencing, authentic assessment, and reflective practice, through which curriculum and assessment design make disciplinary embeddedness educationally operative. The framework repositions academic integrity as a process of scholarly formation rather than compliance, with disciplinary lecturers as key but not exclusive agents. Implications for curriculum design, institutional policy, and future research are discussed in the context of generative AI.

items.title: Discussions on AI Governance in a Fragmented Landscape: Human Rights and the Future of Global AI Governance
items.abstract: On 21 May 2026, the TUM Institute for Ethics in Artificial Intelligence, the Institute of Orthodox Theology at Ludwig Maximilian University, the University of Vienna, and the Ludwig Boltzmann Institute of Fundamental and Human Rights convened a closed-door expert roundtable on “AI Governance in a Fragmented Landscape” at the TUM Think Tank in Munich. The purpose of the roundtable was to discuss how rights-based AI governance can advance while being defined simultaneously by rapid technological change and by deepening geopolitical fragmentation, and to inform the further development of a United Nations (UN) Convention on AI, Data and Human Rights, as outlined in the proposed UN Convention on AI, Data and Human Rights (henceforth referred to as the ‘Munich Convention’). The following report summarizes the main insights from the discussions in Munich, focusing on the drivers and consequences of current geopolitical fragmentation on AI. Furthermore, the report addresses how emerging technological innovations are reshaping human rights. Based on its findings, the report makes a strong call for anchoring AI global governance in human rights through a binding instrument, that addresses impact of AI in a comprehensive way.

items.title: Dream Implementation Science: A Conceptual and Foundational Framework for Transforming Human Aspirations into Real-World Achievements
items.abstract: Human beings continuously formulate dreams, aspirations, ambitions, and objectives. These may involve obtaining an education, developing a scientific discovery, establishing a business, achieving financial independence, improving health, or contributing to society. Despite the importance of these aspirations, the transition from wanting an outcome to actually achieving it remains a complex process involving motivation, knowledge, planning, resources, decision-making, coordination, execution, adaptation, and evaluation. Existing scientific disciplines investigate different components of this process. Goal-setting theory examines the relationship between goals and task performance; implementation-intention research investigates the translation of intentions into action; behavioral science studies motivation and human behavior; operations research investigates resource allocation and optimization; implementation science examines the integration of evidence-based practices into real-world settings; and artificial intelligence enables increasingly sophisticated planning and execution capabilities. However, a broader interdisciplinary framework is needed to investigate the complete lifecycle of human aspirations, from their initial formulation to the achievement and verification of intended outcomes, particularly where individuals, organizations, artificial intelligence systems, and physical technologies must collaborate. This paper proposes Dream Implementation Science (DIS) as an emerging interdisciplinary research field concerned with the scientific study of methods, theories, models, systems, and technologies for transforming human aspirations into achievable and measurable real-world outcomes. The paper introduces a proposed scientific definition, research scope, foundational principles, theoretical foundations, conceptual framework, scientific constructs, mathematical representations, operational models, applications, technological architecture, research methodologies, and evaluation criteria. A central proposition of this framework is that dream implementation should be studied as a dynamic, resource-constrained, feedback-driven, and potentially collaborative process rather than simply an individual act of motivation or goal setting. The framework proposes an integrated lifecycle comprising aspiration identification, objective formalization, feasibility assessment, planning, resource acquisition, execution orchestration, monitoring, adaptation, outcome verification, and sustained achievement. The paper also identifies foundational research questions and proposes future research branches, including Dream Planning Science, Dream Resource Science, Dream Execution Science, Dream Orchestration Science, and Dream Achievement Verification. The framework is conceptual and requires empirical testing. Its purpose is to establish a foundation for a future research program and a possible interdisciplinary scientific discipline.

items.title: Educational-value beliefs and motivational regulation in teachers’ intentions to engage in arts-based practices
items.abstract: Arts-based practices offer teachers creative, participatory, and flexible ways of enriching teaching and learning, yet their educational use may reflect perceived capability, educational-value beliefs, motivational quality, and professional context. This study examined arts-related self-efficacy, different forms of motivational regulation, educational-value beliefs, and perceived school support within an individual–contextual framework, focusing on their associations with teachers’ arts-based engagement intention and on differences between teachers with and without prior arts-related training. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with 408 in-service teachers in Greece (convenience sample); 302 of them were also analyzed in an earlier publication that did not include educational-value beliefs, school support, or training. Reliability, factor-analytic, and discriminant-validity evidence was generally supportive, although the four-construct confirmatory model showed marginal fit and intrinsic motivation and identified regulation were almost indistinguishable at the latent level. Teachers reported high intention, educational-value beliefs, intrinsic motivation, and identified regulation and low amotivation, with marked ceiling and floor effects. In a simultaneous regression (R 2 = 0.338), educational-value beliefs (β = 0.32) and intrinsic motivation (β = 0.29) were the strongest unique correlates of intention; introjected regulation made a small contribution (β = 0.12, about 1% unique variance) that should be interpreted cautiously. Self-efficacy, school support, identified regulation, external regulation, and amotivation showed no unique associations, and in a hierarchical analysis the association of self-efficacy disappeared once motivational regulation was entered. Teachers who reported prior arts-related training scored higher on most study variables (|d| = 0.33–0.82), but training was a single self-reported yes/no item, comparisons were unadjusted, and the cross-sectional design precludes causal conclusions. Prospective engagement with arts-based practices appears to be closely associated with the educational value teachers attribute to such practices and with the quality of their motivation; whether professional learning that offers meaningful, personally engaging encounters with the arts strengthens these orientations remains a question for longitudinal and intervention research.

items.title: End-to-End Evaluation of AI, Agentic AI, and Autonomous Cybersecurity Systems
items.abstract: This paper evaluates artificial intelligence (AI), Agentic AI, and autonomous AI as complete cybersecurity workflows. The paper makes three major contributions: (1) a hierarchical role-and-assurance taxonomy and cross-family synthesis that maps statistical analytics, deep learning, graph neural networks, large language models, and Agentic AI to distinct cybersecurity lifecycle roles; (2) an end-to-end, complete-workflow evaluation framework that integrates precision, recall, F1, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), latency, cost, drift, robustness, unsafe-action rates, escalation, rollback, and auditability; and (3) an empirical synthesis that identifies where modern AI delivers measurable gains over earlier analytics and defines the human-governed safeguards required for bounded, reversible autonomy. Accuracy alone can conceal delay, cost, tool misuse, policy violations, and irreversible actions. Evidence shows F1 = 97.36%, AUROC = 99.59%, and 0.0476 ms latency; drift adaptation increased F1 from 0.60 to 0.86; policy-bounded remediation reduced violations from 12.18% to 5.82%; and layered defenses left 8.4% residual indirect prompt-injection vulnerability. Modern AI performs best on heterogeneous, relational, and multi-step tasks; autonomy should expand only when incremental workflow benefit is measured and failures remain detectable, containable, attributable, and reversible. Keywords: cybersecurity, machine learning, graph neural networks, large language models, agentic AI

items.title: Evaluating error risk in Chinese-to-English artificial intelligence translation systems
items.abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) systems and large language models (LLMs) now produce Chinese–English output that usually reads naturally. That output can still contain meaning errors that a reader of the English alone cannot see. We ask which errors current systems make and how this evidence could inform translator education. Stage 1 re-analyses expert error annotations from five evaluation campaigns of the Conference on Machine Translation (WMT, 2020–2023): 75,232 translations of 6,231 Chinese sentences by 63 systems, including GPT-4, annotated by professional translators with the Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM) error typology. We labelled an output high-risk when at least half of its raters marked a major error. Accuracy errors, mainly mistranslation and omission, made up nearly half of all error events (47–48% under three weighting schemes) and three-quarters to four-fifths of major errors. Overall, 38.5% of outputs were high-risk. In every dataset the proportion of high-risk outputs roughly doubled from the shortest to the longest source sentences. Major errors per source character did not rise with length, however, so longer sentences carry more risk because they contain more text. A transparent surface-feature classifier could rank outputs for review (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve, ROC-AUC = 0.67) but could not certify them, and annotation markers left in the public files spuriously raised its ROC-AUC to 0.80. GPT-4 ranked second among 15 systems on identical sources, yet about one in six of its outputs (16.1%) was high-risk. Stage 2 turns these findings into adjustable curriculum weights. Stage 3 specifies a cluster-randomised trial that would need 12–20 class groups, more than a single department can usually provide.

items.title: Evaluation of Cognitive Workload Using P300 Coherence Evoked by Probe Stimuli of Irrelevant Natural Sound
items.abstract: (1) Maintaining an appropriate level of cognitive workload (CWL) is crucial for work safety and efficiency. The purpose of this study is to investigate a CWL measurement method that is adaptive to changes in work situations, can be performed without interruption of primary work tasks, and is more practical than existing methods such as questionnaires. (2) We thus used the irrelevant probe technique to observe P300 amplitude, using natural sounds as the probe stimulus. Because a degradation of response sensitivity can be expected due to the presence of natural sounds that are not related to work, we also investigated whether accuracy could be improved by using coherence, which accounts for the connection between EEG measurement sites. Drone operation was selected as the model of manual control for the main task, and seven participants performed the task at three levels of difficulty. During the main task, 30 auditory probe stimulations using natural sounds were applied, and the P300 amplitudes generated in response to the auditory probe stimulations were derived from Pz, Cz, and Fz. (3) A certain degree of proportional relationship was confirmed at each measurement point depending on the difficulty of the task, although there was some variance. Comparison of coherence between measurement points revealed a certain proportional relationship between changes in task difficulty. (4) These results indicate that CWL could be evaluated with relative consistency using an index such as coherence even using the irrelevant probe method, which is considered to have low sensitivity. These results suggest that it may be possible to evaluate CWL during actual work.

items.title: Exploring Students’ Generative AI Incorporation in Tasks Requiring Internet Searches and Critical Online Reasoning
items.abstract: Since the release of ChatGPT, numerous articles emerged discussing the pros and cons of the implementing of generative AI tools in educational settings, and researchers predominantly investigated teachers’ and students’ use of those tools in terms of frequency, context of use, and perception. Little is known about students’ processes and approaches when incorporating generative AI tools in their internet searches. Our main aim is to identify different use patterns when employing generative AI-tools for solving information problems that require internet searches. To this end, we investigate students’ actual generative AI use while solving information problems that require internet searches. In our study, first-year university students were presented with generic as well as domain-specific information problems and were allowed to use the internet to write a concluding statement regarding the problem. Out of the total sample, 37 students used a generative AI-tool for task completion. Focusing on these students, we developed a rating scheme and analyzed the prompting pattern, the process of incorporating the generative AI-tool in the task completion, and whether statements from the generative AI-tool were checked against other information sources on the internet. We identified five different types of use patterns when incorporating generative AI-tools in in the process of solving information problems that require internet searches. Results further show that about half of the students heavily rely on the tool and barely verify its statements, while the other half is more cautious and aware of potential unreliable information.

items.title: Exploring Students’ Generative AI Incorporation in Tasks Requiring Internet Searches and Critical Online Reasoning
items.abstract: Since the release of ChatGPT, numerous articles emerged discussing the pros and cons of the implementing of generative AI tools in educational settings, and researchers predominantly investigated teachers’ and students’ use of those tools in terms of frequency, context of use, and perception. Little is known about students’ processes and approaches when incorporating generative AI tools in their internet searches. Our main aim is to identify different use patterns when employing generative AI-tools for solving information problems that require internet searches. To this end, we investigate students’ actual generative AI use while solving information problems that require internet searches. In our study, first-year university students were presented with generic as well as domain-specific information problems and were allowed to use the internet to write a concluding statement regarding the problem. Out of the total sample, 37 students used a generative AI-tool for task completion. Focusing on these students, we developed a rating scheme and analyzed the prompting pattern, the process of incorporating the generative AI-tool in the task completion, and whether statements from the generative AI-tool were checked against other information sources on the internet. We identified five different types of use patterns when incorporating generative AI-tools in in the process of solving information problems that require internet searches. Results further show that about half of the students heavily rely on the tool and barely verify its statements, while the other half is more cautious and aware of potential unreliable information.

items.title: FROM BRAND EXPERIENCE TO EWOM INTENTION: EVIDENCE FROM POP-UP STORES
items.abstract: In the digital era, pop-up stores have emerged as experiential retail platforms that facilitate consumer interaction and foster electronic word-of-mouth (eWOM). This study investigates the influence of brand experience in pop-up stores on consumers’ eWOM intention by integrating the Stimulus–Organism–Response (S-O-R) framework. Drawing on prior literature, the research identifies brand personality and cognitive engagement as key mediating variables linking brand experience to behavioral outcomes. Brand experience, structured across sensory, emotional, cognitive, and behavioral dimensions, serves as an external stimulus that shapes consumers’ internal psychological mechanisms. These include the perception of brand personality and the depth of cognitive engagement, both of which significantly impact eWOM intention. The study proposes a conceptual model in which positive brand experiences enhance brand personality recognition and stimulate cognitive processing, ultimately motivating consumers to share brand-related content online. The research provides theoretical insights into the psychological pathways of experience-driven marketing and offers practical implications for optimizing brand communication strategies in O2O contexts. Future research will empirically validate the proposed model through structural equation modeling.
